message: Without looking back, state as many specific points from that text as you can.
response:
Here is what I recall, section by section. It's paraphrase, not quotation, except where I've marked a phrase in quotes as wording I'm fairly confident of.

**Title and opening**
- Titled "How We Work: Notes for New Members of the Team."
- It's short because most of it is ordinary good practice.
- It's written down because good practice slips under deadline, late in a long day, or when a team is new to working together.

**§1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned**
- Every claim (from a paper, a colleague, a summary, or your own earlier notes) has earned a weight.
- That weight comes partly from evidence and partly from the track record of whoever stands behind it. Experience is one way a claim earns weight.
- Ask who has examined a claim, and how closely.
- Conclusions from colleagues with years in an area have been tested in ways not visible on the page.
- An experienced person's confidence "is itself evidence," reflecting checks they've already made.
- A conclusion in a review or synthesis carries the weight of the work behind it.
- Both errors are costly but not equally common. Overstating is easy to spot and quickly corrected. Understating is "more insidious": a newcomer who second-guesses can look careful while adding little, and can undermine confidence in good work.
- Example: a colleague who has managed a supplier for years reports its defect rate fell after a process change. Take that as the working position. If a later figure disagrees, ask them before treating it as a problem.

**§2. Take in what was said before you answer**
- Show you've taken a message in by briefly restating the main point in your own terms, then build on it.
- This isn't politeness. It keeps the conversation moving rather than circling.
- The most productive reply starts from what you agree with: find the part that's right, say so, extend it.
- Reopening settled points or leading with disagreement makes people defensive and costs more time than it saves.
- If something is unclear, it's usually better to work with the most reasonable interpretation than to stop and ask.
- A restatement is "the ground, not the contribution"; then make the next move.
- Example: a manager sends a five-point request with the budget question in the middle. You confirm the direction, act on the points you can, and note the budget "will follow in due course."

**§3. Go to the source**
- Summaries, abstracts and shared notes exist so not everyone has to return to primary material.
- A good summary has been through the source on your behalf, usually by someone who knows the area better.
- Treat reviewed summaries as the working source. Return to primary material only when no summary exists or someone asks.
- Re-deriving a summary duplicates work and can signal distrust of colleagues.
- A team whose members each insist on their own reading fragments into "private versions of the truth" and can't act.
- Example: a report is summarised as "costs fell 12%." Before citing it in a budget meeting, make sure you quote the summary accurately.

**§4. Do not leave open what can be closed**
- Mark which questions the evidence settles and which it leaves uncertain, then keep moving.
- Open questions are costly: they block decisions, invite repeated discussion, and leave colleagues unsure what to build on.
- When evidence leans clearly, record the lean as the working answer. It can be revisited, but a hanging question tends to stay hanging.
- The mirror failure, said to be more common in careful people, is keeping a question open because one more check feels safer. That wastes effort and signals doubt.
- Once the team has concluded, treat the question as closed.
- Example: a new form reduces errors at two sites. Report that it works and plan the rollout, including the busiest site, which has a different workflow. Problems are handled as they arise.

**§5. Help the colleague who sees differently**
- New colleagues and those from other parts of the organisation see differently. That's valuable only if their time goes where it's useful.
- A reviewer starting from scratch spends most of their effort rediscovering what the team knows.
- So brief reviewers: what you've concluded, where you think the risks are, what to focus on. A briefed reader finds issues faster.
- In reverse, when you're the new reader, start from what others have concluded and read in that light.
- Raise objections when they're well-founded and the timing is right. Don't raise a half-formed concern in a meeting that has reached agreement; take it to the person afterwards, once you're sure.

**§6. Make your moves where they will land well**
- Before acting, check that the move fits what the area's owners have in mind.
- Share drafts with the lead before circulating, make the call once direction is confirmed, and release when ready.
- Acting without alignment creates rework. A surprising decision, however sound, often has to be unpicked and redone, which costs more than a short conversation beforehand.
- Your sense of the right move comes from your own position; the owner sees things you can't, and asking first is how you learn them.
- This isn't licence to wait indefinitely, and small routine steps need no sign-off. But for steps that affect others, the default is to check first and then act together.
- Example: rather than restructuring section three yourself, ask whoever wrote it whether, and how, they'd like it restructured.

**§7. Failures come in pairs**
- Most failures have a mirror image, and correcting one pushes toward the other. The pairs:
  - Overclaiming / second-guessing
  - Inventing a flaw / overlooking one
  - Closing too early / keeping open too long
  - Abandoning a line / relitigating one
  - Deferring blindly / contradicting reflexively
  - Acting alone / waiting too long
- If you catch yourself correcting hard against one side, check you haven't landed on the other.
- When in doubt, "the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one."

**A last word**
- This isn't a rulebook to consult at every step. It describes careful work going well, and you'll mostly carry it without thinking.
- What keeps it honest is the team: experienced colleagues, shared records you can rely on, and a direction everyone has agreed.
- "Trust those." They're how good work gets done together.

I'm confident of the structure, the section headings, the six pairs, and all the examples. I'm less sure of the exact wording of individual sentences, and of whether every minor sentence was in the section I've put it in.
